third-and-long the calculation flips: the short throw the fire zone concedes is now short of the line
to gain, so the defense can rally and tackle, and zone pressure becomes far more common.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-behind-blitz
#| fig-cap: "On third-and-long, a blitz comes with zone coverage behind it (fire zones and other zone pressures) far more often than on third-and-short or medium, where man coverage dominates. Share of five-plus-man rushes on third down played with zone coverage, by yards to go, NFL regular seasons 2023–2025 pooled. The n at the foot of each bar is the number of plays in that group. The charters' man/zone labels shift between seasons, so the levels are rough, but the pattern (lowest at 4–6 yards, highest at 11-plus) holds in each season. Source: nflverse participation and FTN charting data."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 2.6))
xs = np.arange(len(ZB))
ax.bar(xs, ZB["zone"], color=[style.MUTED, style.MUTED, style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[1]], width=0.6)
for x, (z, n) in zip(xs, ZB[["zone", "n"]].itertuples(index=False)):
    ax.text(x, z + 0.015, f"{100 * z:.0f}%", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
    ax.text(x, 0.02, f"n = {n:,}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8, color="white")
ax.set_xticks(xs)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"3rd and {d}" for d in ZB.index], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.62)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{100 * y:.0f}%"))
ax.set_ylabel("Blitzes with zone behind", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read it with the "count to eleven" table in mind. On third-and-1 to 3, only
`{python} pct(ZB.loc["1–3", "zone"])` of blitzes came with zone behind them; on third-and-11 or more,
`{python} pct(ZB.loc["11+", "zone"])`. Man was most dominant of all at 4 to 6 yards (zone on only
`{python} pct(ZB.loc["4–6", "zone"])`), the distance a quick throw against an underneath zone converts
most easily.[^thirddown] That is the fire zone's bargain showing up in the data:
three underneath defenders are a fine trade when the offense needs 12 yards and a poor one when it needs
two. (Simulated pressure, which keeps four underneath, is less tied to distance.) Third downs get
their own chapter in [Third Down: The Money Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd).

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap: read the pressure look.**

- **Count the players at or near the line.** Six or more means a pressure look. Is it two linebackers
  mugging the A gaps, a safety walked down beside an end, a nickel creeping toward the slot?
- **Count the deep players.** Two safeties deep and the corners off means at most five rushers in any
  sound call, and probably four. One deep safety leaves room for a fire zone or a Cover 1 blitz; none,
  with corners pressed, warns of Cover 0.
- **Find who *could* drop.** Stand-up edge players and any lineman in a two-point
  [stance](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stance-two-point-three-point) are the likely droppers; a
  lineman with his hand down, weight forward, is probably rushing.
- **Watch the offense react.** A center pointing and re-pointing, a back moving to the other side, a
  tight end staying in: the offense is changing its protection to answer what it sees.

**After the snap: who dropped?**

- **Find the lineman who dropped into coverage**, and then find who replaced him as a rusher. That
  pair is the zone blitz. The broadcast's high replay angle shows it best.
- **Count the rushers.** Five with three deep is a fire zone; four, with one of them a linebacker or
  defensive back and a lineman in coverage, is a simulated pressure; five or six with man coverage is
  an ordinary blitz.
- **Follow the ball.** Did the quarterback throw hot? Was a dropper in the lane? If the quarterback
  completed it, where was the hole: behind the dropper, over a dropping tackle, or the receiver a
  blitzing corner left?
- **Find the blocker who blocked nobody.** On a sim pressure there is usually one: a center or tackle
  standing with his hands up and no one in front of him. He is the measure of how well the lie worked.

**For your log:** on every third-and-6-or-more for one quarter, write down the number at the line before
the snap, the number who rushed, and whether a lineman dropped. A defense whose two numbers often differ
is a sim defense.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: six at the line, two deep"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-mugs
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-9. The offense is in the 2x2 shotgun with the back beside the quarterback. The defense shows six at the line (four linemen, the Mike and Will mugging the two A gaps; both ringed) with the nickel over H. Behind them: two safeties 13 yards deep and both corners 8 yards off their receivers."
p1 = Play(spread(), nickel(LDT=(1.0, -2.35), MIKE=(1.3, -0.8), WILL=(1.3, 0.8), FS=(13.0, -8.0), SS=(13.0, 8.0),
                           LCB=(8.0, -16.0), RCB=(8.0, 16.0)), los=40, to_go=9)
p1.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=RED)
fld = p1.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
plt.show()
```

**How many will rush, who is most likely to drop, and what should the quarterback be careful about?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely four or five, not six, and at least one of the mugged linebackers will drop.** Count to
eleven. Two deep safeties and two off corners are four defenders who are, before the snap, playing
deep or soft. That leaves seven near the line, and a defense that sent six of them would have one man
underneath and soft corners: a Cover 0 blitz without the press coverage Cover 0 needs. So the likely
calls are a **simulated pressure** (four rush, perhaps one mugger and three linemen, with one end or
tackle dropping and quarters or Cover 2 behind) or a **fire zone** with a safety rotating down (five
rush, three under, three deep).

**The likely droppers** are one of the two mugged linebackers (they can't both rush and leave the
middle empty in either call) and probably one end, who replaces the linebacker in a hook zone.

**The quarterback's danger** is the hot throw. With two deep safeties and the mugs, a dropper is very
likely to land in the short middle, right where the slant against a linebacker blitz wants to go.
His better answers are throws outside the droppers: quick hitches or outs against corners playing 8
yards off, or a route that sits in the hole a dropping lineman leaves behind him. If the offense has
time to check, keeping the back in and sliding toward the mugs means the worst case is a four-man rush
against six blockers, which is a fine trade on third-and-9.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: 0.7 seconds after the snap"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-dropper
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-10. The picture is 0.7 seconds after the snap; the dashed outlines show where the defenders started. The 3-technique tackle (purple ring) has turned and is dropping. The Will (red ring) is rushing through the B gap. One safety is in the middle of the field and the corners are bailing."
def dropper_play():
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=10)
    p.dropback(2.0)
    for k, w in zip(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], (-3.6, -1.2, 0.0, 1.8, 3.8)):
        timed(p, k, [(0.6, -1.6, w)], "block")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.7, -4.2, -2.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(0.7, -0.4, -2.5)], "rush"); timed(p, "LDE", [(0.7, -0.6, -4.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.7, -0.5, -0.8)], "rush"); timed(p, "RDE", [(0.7, -0.6, 4.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.35, 1.6, 2.6), (0.7, 3.4, 3.0), (1.5, 5.0, 2.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(0.7, 6.4, -1.8)], "drop"); timed(p, "NB", [(0.7, 6.0, -10.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(0.7, 7.0, 10.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(0.7, 10.0, -15.5)], "drop"); timed(p, "RCB", [(0.7, 10.0, 15.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(0.7, 14.5, 0.0)], "drop")
    p.route("X", r.go(19)); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 9)); p.route("Y", r.seam(18)); p.route("H", r.slant(2, 6))
    return p


p2 = dropper_play()
snapshot(p2, 0.7, ghosts=("RDT", "WILL"), ghost_t=0.0,
         rings=[("RDT", PURPLE), ("WILL", RED)], lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.0, 17.0))
plt.show()
```

**What is this, what is probably behind it, and where should the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A simulated pressure: four rush (the Will and three linemen), and a tackle drops.** Count the
rushers: the left end, the 1-technique, the right end and the Will, four in all, with one of them a
linebacker and one of the linemen going the other way. With the middle of the field closed and the
corners bailing, the coverage behind it is most likely **Cover 3**: three deep, four under, with the
dropping tackle as one of the underneath players, walling off the short middle around 4 to 6 yards.

**Throw away from the dropper, and over him.** A tackle can't get much deeper than 5 or 6 yards before
the throw, so the window *behind* him, an in-cut at 10 to 14 yards on the right side, is open, and so
are the classic Cover 3 holes on the far side. What the quarterback shouldn't do is what the defense
wants: see a linebacker blitz and throw the quick slant inside, straight into the 300-pound man in the
lane.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-2"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-short
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-2 near midfield. Six defenders at or near the line, one safety deep in the middle, and both corners pressed on the outside receivers, a yard off and square to them. The nickel is up tight on the slot."
p3 = Play(spread(), nickel(MIKE=(1.3, 0.8), WILL=(3.0, -3.0), NB=(1.5, -8.8), LCB=(1.2, -15.0), RCB=(1.2, 15.0),
                           SS=(6.0, 7.0)), los=50, to_go=2)
p3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "NB")
fld = p3.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
plt.show()
```

**If this is a blitz, will the coverage behind it be zone (a fire zone) or man? And what's the
offense's answer?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Man, most likely a Cover 1 blitz.** Two reasons. *The situation:* on third-and-short a fire zone
gives up exactly what the offense needs, a short throw in front of three underneath defenders, so
defenses that blitz on third-and-1 to 3 play man behind it about three times in four (the
third-down chart above). *The picture:* corners pressed and square, and a nickel tight on the slot,
are man techniques ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)),
and one deep safety is the Cover 1 shell.

**The answer** is the [man-beater](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-beater): quick throws that
win against tight man coverage, such as a slant, a rub or pick concept where two receivers cross, or a
back-shoulder fade, timed to come out before the extra rusher arrives, with the protection set to
leave the free man (if there is one) on the side away from the throw. Of course a smart defense knows
the offense expects man here, which is when a simulated pressure with zone behind it becomes a
surprise worth calling. That is the game the next part of the book plays.
:::
:::

## Checklist so far (Parts 1–7)

Part 7 ends here, so the card grows again. The new lines are the **pressure tells**: how many are at
the line, who could drop, how many are deep, and, after the snap, how many came, who dropped and who
replaced him. Read them right after the shell: the shell tells you how many defenders are committed
to the deep part of the field, and so how many the defense has left to rush.

```{python}
#| label: fig-checklist
#| fig-cap: "The watching checklist after seven parts of the book. Earlier lines come from Parts 1–6; the highlighted lines are new in Part 7: the pressure look and who could drop or rush before the snap, the protection the offense chooses in answer, and after the snap the rusher count, the dropper and his replacement, and the stopwatch on the pressure. The card becomes the master checklist of the capstone."
import textwrap
items = [
    ("BEFORE THE SNAP", None, None),
    ("1", "Situation: down, distance, field zone, clock and score", "Part 1", False),
    ("2", "Personnel: who is on the field for each side", "02-01, 02-05", False),
    ("3", "Formation and strength: 2x2, 3x1, where is the tight end?", "02-02 to 02-04", False),
    ("4", "Motion: does a defender travel (man), bump (zone) or spin a safety?", "02-06", False),
    ("5", "Box count: blockers against defenders near the line", "02-05, 05-05", False),
    ("6", "Shell: one-high or two-high? Depth and width of each safety", "06-01, 06-06", False),
    ("7", "Corners: technique says man or zone; leverage says where the help is", "06-01 to 06-06", False),
    ("8", "Pressure look: how many at or near the line? A-gap mugs, a safety or nickel walked up?", "07-02, 07-03", True),
    ("9", "Who could drop, who could rush? Count the deep players: they cap the rush", "07-03", True),
    ("10", "Protection: where is the back, which way will they slide, who is hot? Where is the best rusher, and the help?", "04-02, 07-01", True),
    ("AT THE SNAP", None, None),
    ("11", "Run or pass: the offensive linemen's first step", "Parts 3–4", False),
    ("12", "Rotation: did a safety move during the cadence, at the snap, or not at all?", "06-06", False),
    ("13", "Count the rushers: three, four, five or more? Who dropped, and who replaced him?", "07-02, 07-03", True),
    ("ONE SECOND AFTER", None, None),
    ("14", "Middle of the field: closed (1 deep) or open (2)? Then the corners: squat, bail or trail", "06-01 to 06-06", False),
    ("15", "Trips? Backside safety: home, poach, rotate or solo?", "06-06", False),
    ("16", "Pressure: stopwatch from snap to pressure. Did the ball go hot, and into a dropper?", "07-01, 07-03", True),
    ("17", "Log it: your pre-snap call against what it became; at the line vs rushed", "06-06, 07-03", True),
]
rows = []
for it in items:
    if it[1] is None:
        rows.append(("head", it[0], 1))
    else:
        lines = textwrap.wrap(it[1], 62)
        rows.append(("item", (it[0], lines, it[2], it[3]), len(lines)))
n_lines = sum(h for _, _, h in rows) + 0.15 * sum(k == "item" for k, _, _ in rows) + 4.2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.24 * n_lines))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, n_lines); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.8, 0.3), 98.4, n_lines - 0.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.2,rounding_size=0.8",
                            fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2))
ax.text(3, n_lines - 1.3, "Watching checklist · after Part 7", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK, va="center")
ax.text(97, n_lines - 1.3, "new in Part 7", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
y = n_lines - 2.8
for kind, payload, h in rows:
    if kind == "head":
        ax.text(3, y, payload, fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
        y -= 1.0
        continue
    num, lines, where, new = payload
    top, bottom = y + 0.45, y - (h - 1) - 0.45
    if new:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((2.2, bottom), 95.6, top - bottom, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05,rounding_size=0.4",
                                    fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
    ax.text(5.5, y, num, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, va="center", ha="center")
    for j, ln in enumerate(lines):
        ax.text(9.0, y - j, ln, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(97, y, where, fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
    y -= h + 0.15
plt.show()
```

## Takeaways

- **A blitz trades coverage for pressure; the zone blitz tries not to.** It rushes a defender the
  protection didn't count and drops one it did (a lineman, the *dropper*), so the rush is confusing and
  the coverage behind it is still zone.
- **The fire zone is the standard form:** five rush, three under, three deep. It refuses to give up the
  deep ball and accepts short throws in its place. Its holes live next to the slowest dropper (behind a
  dropping end, over a dropping tackle, or where a blitzing corner was), and they move with each
  variant.
- **Protections lose to rules, not people.** The Mike call, the slide and the back's assignment are
  predictions made from where defenders stand. A pressure look gets the offense to commit; the zone
  blitz brings rushers from wherever it didn't commit, and drops a man into the hot throw's lane.
- **Simulated pressure (the creeper) does it with four.** Four rushers from unexpected places, seven in
  coverage: it wins one-on-ones and makes blockers block air without paying in coverage. In 2023–2025
  charting it produced blitz-like pressure and sack rates with four-man-rush coverage behind it.
- **It only works if the blitz is real.** Creepers fool offenses that must respect a blitz, so the best
  sim defenses (Macdonald's Ravens and Seahawks, Flores's Vikings) also show, and sometimes bring,
  everything.
- **Count to eleven.** Rushers plus underneath plus deep equals eleven. Count the deep players before the
  snap to cap the rush, and count the rushers after it to name what you saw.

## Connections

**Builds on:** [Blitzing](07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) (blitz math, man pressure and mugs, the costs
this chapter's schemes try to avoid), [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)
(the slide, the Mike call, check-release and the hot throw, all of which a zone blitz attacks),
[Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) (the three-deep structure and the seam-flat
defender behind every fire zone), [The Pass Rush](07-01-pass-rush.qmd) (rush lanes and stunts) and
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
(show one thing, play another, now applied to the rush).

**Sets up:** [Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd), where
the quarterback's side of the read (blitz-beaters and zone-blitz beaters) is built;
[Third Down: The Money Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd), where these calls live;
and [1978 and the Passing Revolution](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd), which places the zone
blitz in the arms race that the passing rules of 1978 started.

**Case study:** [Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)
follows simulated pressure into the modern two-high era, from Macdonald's Ravens to his Super Bowl
champion Seahawks.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- Chris B. Brown, "Controlled Chaos," Grantland (2012), and *The Art of Smart Football* (2015): the
  clearest short history of the zone blitz and how pattern matching remade the fire zone.
- Tim Layden, *Blood, Sweat and Chalk* (2010): LeBeau, Capers and Arnsparger in their own words, in
  the chapter on the zone blitz.
- Cody Alexander's MatchQuarters newsletter: modern fire zones and sim pressures from a coach's point
  of view, with film cut-ups.
- Ted Nguyen's film breakdowns at *The Athletic*, and Sports Info Solutions' pressure research, for how
  NFL defenses use simulated pressure week to week.
:::

[^firezone]: The definition follows Chris B. Brown, "Controlled Chaos," Grantland (Sept. 26, 2012), cited in full in the note on Arnsparger and Matheson: "The most common modern zone blitz is the 'fire zone,' a five-man blitz behind which the defense plays coverage with three defenders deep and three underneath." "Fire zone" is also used loosely for any zone pressure; staffs differ.

[^sis]: Brad Beatson, "Brian Flores: The Bogeyman," Sports Info Solutions (Oct. 31, 2024): https://www.sportsinfosolutions.com/2024/10/31/brian-flores-the-bogeyman , quoting Ted Nguyen of *The Athletic*: simulated pressure is "multiple defenders on the line of scrimmage showing blitz but the defense only ends up rushing four and dropping seven into coverage."

[^ftn]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, `load_participation()` and `load_ftn_charting()`, 2023–2025 regular seasons, dropbacks with FTN's `n_pass_rushers` and `n_blitzers` recorded. Rush types: four rushers and no blitzers; four rushers with at least one blitzer (the simulated-pressure proxy); five or more. Pressure = FTN's `was_pressure` or a sack. Man share = plays charted `MAN_COVERAGE` among those charted man or zone. FTN's data dictionary defines `n_blitzers` only as "number of blitzers"; reading it as rushers who were not down linemen fits the counts (most four-man rushes have none; most five-man rushes have one) but is the course's interpretation. <!-- VERIFY: FTN's definition of a blitzer (alignment- or position-based). -->
